implementation_notes: Scala's mixin composition replaces the classic Decorator/Interceptor skeleton: a trait that extends the same base type declares abstract override def pay(...) = { audit; super.pay(...) }, and mixing it in after a concrete implementation wraps that implementation - stacking several such traits yields the interceptor chain, and linearization decides the order. For HTTP or actor stacks the framework seam is usually better (Play action composition, Akka's aroundReceive), and annotation-driven interception requires an AspectJ-style weaver, which is an extra build dependency rather than a language feature.
pitfalls: abstract override only compiles when the trait is mixed in after a concrete implementation; a class that lacks a concrete pay() fails at compile time, and mixing order changes which wrapper runs first (last mixin wins).
super in a stackable trait resolves through linearization, so the auditing trait behaves differently depending on the class it is mixed into - document the expected stack, do not assume it.
A trait cannot carry per-instance construction state cleanly; the sink usually arrives through a self-type or a protected member, which makes the trait harder to use standalone.
